doc.title: Nicki Parrott interviewed by Monk Rowe. Utica, New York, November 6, 2010 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Dressing and being taken seriously as a young woman bassist
summary: She once dressed like a guy, was turned down when a caller learned Nick was a woman, and now sees an even playing field.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Is there a double standard for the way a woman musician has to try to look on a gig as opposed to guys. I mean guys can, I don’t know if guys think that much about what they wear.

No they don’t. Sometimes it’s really obvious with musicians that they really put no thought, in fact that shirt and that tie, really? I mean it’s not about fashion, you know, playing music, but it is about looking presentable. And it’s good to definitely look presentable. Getting back to your point, getting back to the question again, sorry.
I just wondered if you feel like you have to pay more attention to how you dress.

No I used to try to dress way more like a guy when I was first starting out in music. Oh yeah. And I was so conscious of not being taken seriously. There was one instance when I got called for a gig and they said, “Is this Nick Parrott?” And I said, “Well actually it’s Nicki.” “A bass player?” “Yeah, Nicki Parrott.” Click. You know what I mean? So it was like instances where I was like really fragile. I was still trying to learn how to play. And I was 18 or 19 and I noticed that guys I grew up with in Newcastle were getting all these great gigs and it was the first time I was aware that, oh God, I’m a woman in this business. You know what I mean? It was like the first time I’d really become aware of this is going to be different for me, to them, in a way. It was like subtle differences. But I’ve been one of the lucky ones though. I’ve been a professional musician for, like I said, for basically 22 years with an eight month stint in fashion. In these days it doesn’t matter, you know, woman, man, black, white, anything. It’s just a more difficult time to be a musician. So all of that stuff is gone by the wayside because economically it’s a challenge whoever you are. It doesn’t matter anymore. That’s how I feel now. I feel it’s pretty much an even playing field, you know what I mean, where there are gigs to be had and you have to work really hard at getting them it seems.
